title: Week 2: Census data mining
text:
Had a quiz, setup portfolio notes for today, had a lesson about dplyr and the census, and had practice (week2.R), learned about several key functions, analyzed incomes of counties in PA.

Loaded tidyverse and tidycensus, then downloaded 2023 ACS five-year median household income for Pennsylvania counties.
Used dim(), glimpse(), and head() to inspect the number of rows, columns, variable types, and first observations.
Practiced the main dplyr verbs. Each verb takes a rectangular table and returns another table:

filter() chooses rows.
select() chooses columns.
mutate() creates or changes columns.
arrange() sorts rows; desc() sorts in descending order.
group_by() and summarize() turn many rows into one row per group.
count() counts observations in each category.

Calculated relative margin of error and saved the result:


pa_income <- pa_income %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

mutate() only prints a temporary result unless it is assigned back to an object with <-.

Used case_when() to create reliability categories:


pa_income <- pa_income %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 3 ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 6 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE        ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

The conditions are checked from top to bottom. The final TRUE means everything that did not match an earlier condition.

Compared long and wide ACS data. With two variables in the default long format, each county has two rows. With output = "wide", each county has one row and the variables appear side by side. In wide ACS data, E means estimate and M means margin of error.

Original quick notes (kept)

arrange(step1, desc(moe_pct))
select(NAME, moe_pct)
mutate(new_col = col1 / col2)

Magrittr pipe: %>%

The pipe means “and then.” It passes the result from one step into the next step and should go at the end of the line.

  filter(moe_pct > 5) %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct)


GEOID is an identifier, not a quantity. It should stay as character data because converting it to a number removes leading zeros.

title: Week 7: Spatial Autocorrelation in Errors
text:
Reviewed how to read a logged predictor. If X is logged but Y stays in dollars, then beta / 100 is the approximate change in Y for a 1% increase in X.
Moved from census tracts to individual house sales. For point data, we can create spatial features with buffers or nearest neighbors:

buffer VS KNN -> spatial lag
A buffer can count events within a fixed distance, such as violent crimes within 660 feet.
k-nearest neighbors (kNN) can measure the average distance to the nearest events. It can also define the neighbors used for a spatial lag.
We should compare these features using cross-validation RMSE.

Cleaned the sales data. Very low sale prices may represent family transfers, sheriff sales, or other non-market transactions, so the cleaning rule must be explained.
Fit a house-price model and calculated the errors:


m1 <- lm(
  sale_price ~ total_livable_area + number_of_bathrooms + age + violent_knn5,
  data = sales
)

sales <- sales %>%
  mutate(
    pred = predict(m1, sales),
    resid = sale_price - pred
  )

A positive residual means the actual price is higher than the predicted price, so the model under-predicted. A negative residual means the model over-predicted.

Map the errors. A residual map helps show where similar errors may cluster. Using alpha and squish keeps overlapping points and very large errors from hiding the main pattern.
Created a spatial lag using the five nearest houses:


coords <- st_coordinates(sales)
w_knn <- nb2listw(
  knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 5)),
  style = "W"
)

sales$resid_lag <- lag.listw(w_knn, sales$resid)

The spatial lag is the average residual of a house’s five nearest neighbors.

Used Moran’s I to measure whether the residuals cluster in space:

\[
I = \frac{n}{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}}
    \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i-\bar{x})(x_j-\bar{x})}
    {\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})^2}
\]
My short version of the idea is:

w_ij -> 1(neighbor); 0(non-neighbor)
reference point -> x_i; compare each observation with its neighbors.
[-1, 1] -> -1(more sparse); 0(random scatter); 1(cluster) In clearer terms, values near -1 show dispersion, values near 0 show little spatial pattern, and values near 1 show clustering of similar values.


Used a permutation test for significance:


mc <- moran.mc(sales$resid, w_knn, nsim = 499)
mc$statistic
mc$p.value

Significance test: shuffle -> p-value. The test shuffles residuals among houses many times. If the observed Moran’s I is more extreme than almost all shuffled values, the spatial pattern is unlikely to be random.

If Moran’s I is high and significant: the model is probably missing something about place. Possible improvements include a new spatial feature, a neighborhood fixed effect, or an interaction. After adding features, refit the model and compare both CV RMSE and Moran’s I.

title: Week 7: Spatial Autocorrelation in Errors
text:
Key Concepts
This lecture introduced spatial autocorrelation as a model diagnostic. A residual is actual - predicted, and a residual map shows where the model under-predicts or over-predicts. A spatial lag summarizes nearby values, while Moran’s I measures whether similar residuals are close together. Moran’s I near 1 means clustering, near 0 means little spatial pattern, and below 0 means neighboring values tend to differ. A small p-value tells us the pattern is unlikely to be random, but with a large sample almost everything can be significant, so the size of Moran’s I is also important.
For prediction, we should build spatial features from X variables, such as nearby crime or distance to an amenity, rather than using nearby Y values such as house prices. Using neighbors’ prices can create data leakage during cross-validation.

title: Week 7: Spatial Autocorrelation in Errors
text:
Reflection
This lecture helped me see that RMSE alone does not show where a model is wrong. Two models can have similar RMSE, but one may have strongly clustered errors. If nearby houses are all under-predicted or all over-predicted, the model is missing some local information. Mapping residuals and calculating Moran’s I therefore gives a clearer way to decide what feature to add next. I also learned that a significant p-value is not enough; the goal is to make Moran’s I smaller while also improving prediction error.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data and Indego Access
text:
Original quick notes (kept)

1. left.join(tableA, tableB, by="column")  # `left.join` makes wider table with tableA on the left

2. get_acs(... , geometry = TRUE)
*by the way, the original `get_acs` is:
  get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = "B19013_001",
    state = 'PA',
    year = 2023,
    survey = "acs5"
  )
  
3. Coordinate Reference System (CRS)
shape, area, distance, direction
conformal conic (Lambert): ideal for mid-lontitude countries
cylindrical: ideal for world map
State Plane Coordinate System: more precise, special to US
EPSG:4326：WGS84                        degrees
EPSG:2272: PA Sourthern (state plane)   feets/meters
EPSG:5070: Albers equal area            meters
EPSG:4269: NAD83                        degrees
UTM grid: Mercato(N80 to S80, 60zones)

4. st_crs(data)
st_set.crs()  # add the crs label to the geometru column
st_transform(data, 2272)

Judgement functions:
st_intersects() # any commom point or line
st_touches()    # touches but no overlapped area inside
st_within()

Action functions:
st_filter()     # count the tracts
st_intersection() # return intersected area
st_union()      # union two area, return one
st_join()
st_distance()   # return a matrix



Attribute join:


left_join(tableA, tableB, by = "column")

left_join() makes a wider table while keeping every row from tableA on the left. This is a join by a shared attribute such as GEOID.

Downloaded ACS geography:


get_acs(..., geometry = TRUE)

# The original get_acs example was:
get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B19013_001",
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

An sf object is a data frame with an extra geometry column. Each row is still one place, so regular dplyr functions still work. The geometry column is sticky: use st_drop_geometry() when a plain table is needed.

Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS) describe shape, area, distance, and direction:

Conformal conic (Lambert): useful for mid-latitude countries or regions.
Cylindrical: useful for some world maps.
State Plane Coordinate System: a precise system designed for areas within the United States.
EPSG:4326: WGS84, measured in degrees.
EPSG:2272: NAD83 / Pennsylvania South, measured in US feet.
EPSG:5070: Albers equal area, measured in meters.
EPSG:4269: NAD83, measured in degrees.
UTM grid: a Mercator-based system from about 80°S to 84°N, divided into 60 zones.


For this project, a simple rule is: store or share data in EPSG:4326, but calculate Philadelphia distances and buffers in EPSG:2272.

Checked and changed CRS information:


st_crs(data)
st_crs(data)$units
st_set_crs(data, 2272)   # add or correct a missing CRS label
st_transform(data, 2272) # convert the coordinates

st_set_crs() changes the CRS label without moving the geometry. st_transform() actually converts coordinates. Before comparing or measuring two layers, check that they use the same projected CRS and the expected units.

Judgment functions:

st_intersects() — do two shapes share any point or area?
st_touches() — do the boundaries touch without overlapping interiors?
st_within() — is one shape completely within another?


These functions return relationships. For example, st_intersects() returns a list, and lengths() can turn that list into a count for each feature.

Action functions:

st_filter() — keep whole features that match a spatial condition.
st_intersection() — cut shapes and return the overlapping area.
st_union() — combine multiple shapes into one shape.
st_join() — join rows according to spatial location.
st_distance() — return a matrix of distances between every pair of features.
st_nearest_feature() — return the index of the nearest feature.
st_buffer() — create an area around a feature using the CRS units.

Used three possible definitions of access to Indego stations:

The tract centroid is within one-half mile of a station.
The tract touches a station service buffer.
At least a chosen percentage of the tract area is covered by the service zone.


These definitions can produce different results. Choosing a spatial predicate is a policy and analytical decision, not only a technical choice.

Checked the results. A station on a tract boundary may be counted twice, while a station outside the tract layer may be counted zero times. Row counts, missing values, CRS, units, and totals should be checked before reporting an answer.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data and Indego Access
text:
Key Concepts
This lab introduced spatial data analysis in R using sf. Key concepts included coordinate reference systems (CRS), spatial joins, distance calculations, buffers, spatial filtering, and spatial intersections. I learned that st_transform() converts coordinates between CRSs, while st_join() matches observations based on location. We also used st_nearest_feature() and st_distance() to measure distance, and st_buffer() to create station service areas. Finally, we combined spatial operations with regular dplyr joins to identify low-income census tracts without access to Indego stations.
The most important workflow is:

Check the CRS and units.
Transform both layers to the same projected CRS.
Use a spatial join or spatial predicate.
Drop geometry when doing a non-spatial summary.
Join the summary back to the spatial master layer by GEOID when it is time to map.

For maps, use a clear title and legend, light boundaries, theme_void(), and colors that match the meaning of the data. Sequential colors show low-to-high values; diverging colors require a meaningful midpoint such as zero.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data and Indego Access
text:
Reflection
This lab helped me understand how spatial analysis can answer a practical policy question rather than simply produce a map. I found the distinction between joining by an attribute such as GEOID and joining by geographic location especially useful. The different definitions of access also showed me that spatial results depend strongly on methodological choices. For example, using a tract centroid, whether a tract touches a station buffer, or the percentage of tract area covered can produce different conclusions. I also learned that checking CRS, row counts, and missing values is important for avoiding misleading results.

Possible improvements include using the street network, entrances, walking time, barriers, and population distribution within each tract instead of assuming that everyone begins at the centroid.

title: Week 8: LISA and Responsible Modeling
text:
Original quick notes (kept)

1. LISA: Local Indicators of Spatial Association (Local Moran’s I/Getis-Ord/Local Geary’s c)
2. Weight matrix: queen (share a line) / rook (point or line)
3. local Moran's I: center 1 house at a time and calculate her neighbors' average deviation of residuals
4. Residual = actual - predicted:
  High = under predicted, Low = over predicted
  cluster: HH, LL
  outlier: HL. LH



Learned the difference between global and local spatial autocorrelation:

Global Moran’s I gives one number and asks whether errors cluster overall.
Local Moran’s I, a type of LISA, gives one value for every house and shows where errors cluster.

Reviewed spatial weights. For polygons, rook neighbors share an edge, while queen neighbors share an edge or a corner. For house points, we used each house’s five nearest neighbors and row-standardized weights (style = "W").
Used out-of-fold residuals, where each house’s prediction comes from a model that did not train on that house. This gives a more honest picture of model error.
Calculated Local Moran’s I. The basic idea is “my deviation × my neighbors’ average deviation,” with scaling:

\[
I_i = \frac{z_i}{m_2}\sum_j w_{ij}z_j
\]

w_knn <- nb2listw(
  knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(sales), k = 5)),
  style = "W"
)

local_i <- localmoran_perm(sales$resid, w_knn, nsim = 499)


Classified significant observations into four LISA quadrants. Because residual = actual - predicted:

High-High (HH): the house and its neighbors are under-predicted. This may show a missing local amenity.
Low-Low (LL): the house and its neighbors are over-predicted. This may show a missing local disamenity.
High-Low (HL): one under-predicted house among over-predicted neighbors.
Low-High (LH): one over-predicted house among under-predicted neighbors.


HH and LL are spatial clusters that point toward a place. HL and LH are spatial outliers that may point toward a special house or a data problem.

Made a LISA map. For each significant cluster, ask: Where is it? What is there that the model does not know? Can it be measured with open data? The answer can suggest the next model feature.
Compared three ways to define “near”:

Buffer count: number of events within a chosen radius; useful for exposure, but the radius is a choice and many values may be zero.
Nearest distance: distance to the single closest event; useful when one nearby facility matters, but one unusual point can control the result.
kNN mean distance: average distance to the k closest events; smoother and never zero, but k must be chosen.


Choose a short list of reasonable distances or k values before seeing the results, then use cross-validation RMSE to compare them. These should be features of X, not nearby house prices.

Used the model improvement loop:

Fit the model and get out-of-fold residuals.
Check global Moran’s I.
Use the LISA map to locate clusters.
Build a feature that could explain a cluster.
Refit and compare CV RMSE, Moran’s I, and the number of clusters.


If a cluster does not shrink, the idea about what was missing may be wrong. That is still useful information.

Discussed the RealPage rent-pricing case. The important questions were not only whether the regression was accurate, but also what data entered the model, who acted on its recommendations, whether people could override it, and who paid the cost of its decisions.

Global Moran’s I gives one number and asks whether errors cluster overall.
Local Moran’s I, a type of LISA, gives one value for every house and shows where errors cluster.

Reviewed spatial weights. For polygons, rook neighbors share an edge, while queen neighbors share an edge or a corner. For house points, we used each house’s five nearest neighbors and row-standardized weights (style = "W").
Used out-of-fold residuals, where each house’s prediction comes from a model that did not train on that house. This gives a more honest picture of model error.
Calculated Local Moran’s I. The basic idea is “my deviation × my neighbors’ average deviation,” with scaling:

\[
I_i = \frac{z_i}{m_2}\sum_j w_{ij}z_j
\]

w_knn <- nb2listw(
  knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(sales), k = 5)),
  style = "W"
)

local_i <- localmoran_perm(sales$resid, w_knn, nsim = 499)


Classified significant observations into four LISA quadrants. Because residual = actual - predicted:

High-High (HH): the house and its neighbors are under-predicted. This may show a missing local amenity.
Low-Low (LL): the house and its neighbors are over-predicted. This may show a missing local disamenity.
High-Low (HL): one under-predicted house among over-predicted neighbors.
Low-High (LH): one over-predicted house among under-predicted neighbors.


HH and LL are spatial clusters that point toward a place. HL and LH are spatial outliers that may point toward a special house or a data problem.

Made a LISA map. For each significant cluster, ask: Where is it? What is there that the model does not know? Can it be measured with open data? The answer can suggest the next model feature.
Compared three ways to define “near”:

Buffer count: number of events within a chosen radius; useful for exposure, but the radius is a choice and many values may be zero.
Nearest distance: distance to the single closest event; useful when one nearby facility matters, but one unusual point can control the result.
kNN mean distance: average distance to the k closest events; smoother and never zero, but k must be chosen.


Choose a short list of reasonable distances or k values before seeing the results, then use cross-validation RMSE to compare them. These should be features of X, not nearby house prices.

Used the model improvement loop:

Fit the model and get out-of-fold residuals.
Check global Moran’s I.
Use the LISA map to locate clusters.
Build a feature that could explain a cluster.
Refit and compare CV RMSE, Moran’s I, and the number of clusters.


If a cluster does not shrink, the idea about what was missing may be wrong. That is still useful information.

Discussed the RealPage rent-pricing case. The important questions were not only whether the regression was accurate, but also what data entered the model, who acted on its recommendations, whether people could override it, and who paid the cost of its decisions.

title: Week 8: LISA and Responsible Modeling
text:
Key Concepts
LISA means Local Indicators of Spatial Association. Global Moran’s I tells us whether residuals cluster in general, while Local Moran’s I tells us where the clusters and outliers are. A LISA map is therefore a diagnostic and a to-do list for feature building.
Local tests also create a multiple-testing problem because thousands of locations are tested at once, so some clusters may appear by chance. The results should be interpreted with the map, local knowledge, and out-of-sample model performance.
Model quality is not only technical. A model can predict accurately and still cause harm. Three useful questions are:

What is in the data, and who supplied it?
Who acts on the prediction, and can they say no?
Who pays when the prediction is wrong—and when it is right?

title: Week 8: LISA and Responsible Modeling
text:
Reflection
This lecture helped me understand why one global Moran’s I value is not enough. LISA shows the specific neighborhoods where a model repeatedly under-predicts or over-predicts, so it can guide the next spatial feature. I also learned that clusters and outliers suggest different problems: clusters usually point to missing information about place, while outliers may point to an unusual property or a data-quality issue. The RealPage example showed that an accurate model can still be harmful depending on its data, users, incentives, and consequences.

title: Week 8: LISA and Responsible Modeling
text:
Questions I Still Have
How sensitive are LISA clusters to the choice of k, the weight matrix, and the significance level? How should multiple local tests be corrected without hiding meaningful small clusters?

Our Y is an ACS estimate with its own margin of error. Add the residuals to the table and check whether the biggest misses happen where the estimate is least reliable.

  mutate(fitted_m2 = fitted(m2),
         resid_m2  = residuals(m2))

  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "CV of the median rent estimate (%)",
       y = "Size of the model's miss ($)",
       title = "Are the biggest misses in the noisiest tracts?") +
  theme_minimal()








Stop and look: If a tract’s rent estimate has a CV of 35%, how much of the model’s miss there could be survey noise rather than a model failure? What does that mean for flagging “tracts with rents above expectation”?

your answer:
With a CV of 35%, the 90% margin of error is about ±58% of the rent estimate — roughly ±$576 on a $1,000 rent, more than twice the model’s typical miss of $261. So in such a tract the whole residual could be survey noise rather than model failure. Flagging should require the positive residual to exceed the estimate’s own margin of error (residual > 1.645 × CV × rent); high-CV tracts are fog, not signal.

WarningTwo different CVs



Week 3 CV = coefficient of variation: how noisy is one estimate? Today’s CV = cross-validation: how well does a model predict data it hasn’t seen? Same letters, unrelated ideas.



6A: One train/test split

train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

Part 8: The Challenge
Your team’s job: build the best model for predicting tract median rent, then use it to answer the agency’s question.

Rules

The grade is 10-fold CV RMSE. Use model_df (or tracts) and run set.seed(5080) directly before train(), exactly as in Part 6B, so every team is tested on the same folds.
Don’t drop rows. If you add a variable with missing values, you change the folds and the comparison stops being fair. Fill the gaps or choose a different variable.
You may add any ACS variables (use load_variables(2023, "acs5") to browse) and any spatial feature you can build with Week 4 tools: distances, buffers, counts.
You may not use anything built from rent itself. That rules out med_rentM, rent_cv, rent burden (B25071), and the rent distribution tables (B25063). Ask yourself: would the agency have this variable for a tract whose rent it’s trying to predict? If not, using it is cheating the test. That’s called leakage.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
The article
I am using Option A, the provided article: Alfred Lubrano, “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty”, WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer, December 6, 2018.
It compares the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS 5-year estimates and makes several specific claims:

Citywide poverty stood at 26 percent.
Fairhill had a 61 percent poverty rate.
Eastwick jumped from 12 to 26 percent, the largest rise of any neighborhood.
Holmesburg rose from 2 to 19 percent; Mayfair from 1 to 14 percent.
Poverty rose in 22 majority-white neighborhoods.

Census tracts are not neighborhoods, and the article never published which tracts went into which neighborhood, so I work at the tract level for Philadelphia County. My numbers will not match the article’s exactly — that is expected, not a failure.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Part 1: Reconstruct the data
I pull table B17001 at the tract level: B17001_002 (population below the poverty level) over B17001_001 (population for whom poverty status is determined). A poverty rate needs a numerator and a denominator, and its margin of error has to be propagated from both with moe_prop() — it does not carry over from the count. I use survey = "acs5" with year = 2010 (the 2006–2010 window) and year = 2017 (2013–2017), the two periods the article names, because tract-level estimates only exist in the 5-year ACS and the article says it used the five-year figures.
The article forces a few assumptions on me: it publishes no tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk, so tract level is as far as I can go; Philadelphia County (state 42, county 101) matches the city boundary; tracts are matched across periods by GEOID; and any tract with a zero or missing denominator gets NA instead of an invalid rate. The two windows share no calendar years, so the two estimates are independent, and the standard MOE for a difference — sqrt(MOE1² + MOE2²) — is exactly right here. If the windows overlapped, the estimates would be positively correlated and that formula would overstate the MOE of the change.


Show code
poverty_vars <- c(
  below_poverty = "B17001_002",
  total         = "B17001_001"
)

acs_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = poverty_vars,
  state  = 42,
  county = 101,
  year   = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

acs_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = poverty_vars,
  state  = 42,
  county = 101,
  year   = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

n_distinct(acs_2010$GEOID)


[1] 384

Both periods return 384 tracts.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Part 2: Test the change
For each tract and period I compute the poverty rate and its MOE with moe_prop(), setting the rate to NA wherever the denominator is zero or missing.


Show code
poverty_2010 <- acs_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2006_2010",
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate     = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate, NA_real_),
    poverty_rate_moe = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate_moe, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)

poverty_2017 <- acs_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2013_2017",
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate     = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate, NA_real_),
    poverty_rate_moe = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate_moe, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)

poverty_wide <- bind_rows(poverty_2010, poverty_2017) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = period,
    values_from = c(poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)
  )


Each ACS MOE is at 90 percent confidence, so the standard error is MOE / 1.645. The change is the difference of the two rates, its MOE is sqrt(MOE1² + MOE2²), and the change counts as statistically detectable when the z-score clears the 90 percent critical value of 1.645. I also compute each estimate’s coefficient of variation (SE / estimate × 100) and flag reliability with the Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds: CV < 12 reliable, 12–40 somewhat reliable, > 40 unreliable.


Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change   = poverty_rate_2013_2017 - poverty_rate_2006_2010,
    se_1     = poverty_rate_moe_2006_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2     = poverty_rate_moe_2013_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    cv_2006_2010 = se_1 / poverty_rate_2006_2010 * 100,
    cv_2013_2017 = se_2 / poverty_rate_2013_2017 * 100,
    reliability_2006_2010 = case_when(
      is.na(cv_2006_2010) ~ NA_character_,
      cv_2006_2010 < 12   ~ "reliable",
      cv_2006_2010 <= 40  ~ "somewhat reliable",
      TRUE                ~ "unreliable"
    ),
    reliability_2013_2017 = case_when(
      is.na(cv_2013_2017) ~ NA_character_,
      cv_2013_2017 < 12   ~ "reliable",
      cv_2013_2017 <= 40  ~ "somewhat reliable",
      TRUE                ~ "unreliable"
    )
  )


Eight tracts come back NA. Before deciding what to do with them, I checked why.


Show code
poverty_tested %>%
  filter(is.na(change)) %>%
  left_join(acs_2010 %>% select(GEOID, total_2010 = totalE), by = "GEOID") %>%
  left_join(acs_2017 %>% select(GEOID, total_2017 = totalE), by = "GEOID") %>%
  select(NAME, total_2010, total_2017)

All eight are zero-population special-use tracts — Tract 50 plus the 9800-series (9803–9809), which in Philadelphia cover institutional and non-residential land such as the airport. Their population with poverty status determined is zero in both periods, so a poverty rate is undefined, not merely noisy. I exclude them and test the remaining 376.


Show code

  summarise(
    total_tracts    = n(),
    excluded_na     = sum(is.na(significant)),
    detectable      = sum(significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    not_detectable  = sum(!significant, na.rm = TRUE),

    avg_rate_2013_2017 = mean(poverty_rate_2013_2017) * 100,

Of 376 testable tracts, only 63 (17 percent) show a change distinguishable from zero at 90 percent confidence — 36 up, 27 down. The other 313 (83 percent) could easily not have changed at all.
The average tract poverty rate did drift up, from 25.5 to 26.1 percent — which squares with the article’s citywide “26 percent” — and 22 tracts still sit above 55 percent, so the concentrated, Fairhill-style poverty the article describes is real. But a city where five tracts in six show no detectable change is mostly flat, not surging. One artifact needs a flag: the largest single “decrease” is special-use Tract 9800 (about 84 → 5 percent, group-quarters population), and special-use tracts 9891 and 9801 carry MOEs of ±221 and ±163 points, so the error-bar plot below clips its axis.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Part 3: Adjudicate the claims
Supported. The citywide level checks out: my average tract rate for 2013–2017 is 26.1 percent against the article’s “26 percent,” up from 25.5 in 2006–2010. The direction is right too: among tracts with detectable change, increases (36) outnumber decreases (27), and the median change is +1.2 points. And concentrated, Fairhill-style poverty is real — 22 tracts exceed 55 percent, several in the mid-60s.
Not supported. The “startling surge” framing overstates what five-year tract data can show: 313 of 376 tracts (83 percent) are statistically indistinguishable from no change at all. Apparent jumps from very low baselines — exactly the Holmesburg (2%) and Mayfair (1%) pattern — are the least trustworthy numbers in the ACS: 44 tracts had unreliable 2006–2010 estimates (CV > 40), and a poverty rate of 1–2 percent typically carries an error band several times its size. Quoting “1 to 14 percent” without a margin of error is quoting endpoints of a noisy interval.
Cannot be determined. Every named-neighborhood figure — Fairhill 61%, Eastwick 12→26%, Holmesburg 2→19%, Mayfair 1→14% — would require the article’s tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk, which it never published. The “22 majority-white neighborhoods” claim additionally needs poverty by race and a definition of majority-white. The white-poverty jump (14.8 → 19.4 percent) comes from a one-year survey, a different data product than the five-year comparison. The median-income claims rest on other tables I did not test.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Part 4: Rewrite the central paragraph
New five-year Census estimates paint a sobering but more nuanced picture of Philadelphia. Averaged across the city’s 384 census tracts, the poverty rate in 2013–2017 was about 26 percent, up modestly from 2006–2010. The average hides extremes: in more than 20 tracts, poverty exceeds 55 percent — echoing the deprivation reported in Fairhill — and eight tracts saw statistically confirmed increases of 20 percentage points or more. Yet most of the city did not measurably move: in 313 of 376 testable tracts, the change was too small to distinguish from sampling error. Because the American Community Survey is a sample, small-area figures carry wide margins of error — especially where poverty is rare — so dramatic neighborhood-level jumps deserve skepticism before they are believed.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
For Illinois, I’ve chosen to examine median home value (variable B25077_001). Housing markets vary dramatically across the state, from Chicago’s urban core to rural farming counties, but ACS estimates in sparsely populated areas often come with wider margins of error. I want to assess not only where property values are highest, but also which counties’ estimates are statistically reliable enough to inform housing policy or investment decisions.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
What: The communities we know the least about in Illinois are its smallest, most rural counties. From my analysis, the 27 Low confidence counties—which include sparsely populated areas like Hardin, Pope, Calhoun, and Gallatin counties—have an average population of just 11,301 residents. These are precisely the places where ACS estimates are most unreliable, yet they represent a significant portion of Illinois’s geographic area.
Why: The survey is sample‑based, not a census, and reliability depends heavily on sample size. Smaller counties contribute fewer respondents, which produces wider margins of error around every estimate. The ACS’s own design prioritizes precision for larger populations, leaving rural communities with statistically noisy data.
Who: If a state agency distributing housing grants based on median home values, treating every county’s estimate as equally certain. Using the 27 Low confidence counties’ numbers at face value could misdirect funds—a county with an artificially high estimate might receive less aid than it actually needs, while another with a low estimate might be overlooked despite hidden poverty. The rural poor, already underserved, would be the ones hurt most.

Optional challenge: one function, five states
The county-level pull earlier in this report is hard-coded to one state. I wrapped it in a function, pull_county_reliability(), that takes a state abbreviation (plus optional variable and year) and returns each county’s estimate, margin of error, population, and moe_pct:

pull_county_reliability <- function(state_abbr, variable = "B25077_001", year = 2023) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = c(myvar = variable, pop = "B01003_001"),
    state = state_abbr,
    year = year,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide"
  ) %>%
    transmute(
      state = state_abbr,
      GEOID,
      NAME,
      estimate = myvarE,
      moe = myvarM,
      popE,
      moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100
    )
}

With purrr::map_dfr() the same analysis runs across several states at once. I picked five with very different settlement geographies: Illinois, Ohio, Georgia, Montana, and Wyoming — 428 counties in total.

states <- c("IL", "OH", "GA", "MT", "WY")

multi_state <- map_dfr(states, pull_county_reliability)

multi_state %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 3  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 7  ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  )) %>%
  group_by(state, reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

The rule is universal, but its footprint depends on settlement geography: states dominated by small rural counties simply have less trustworthy home-value data overall than states of evenly mid-sized counties like Ohio.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.








Important2. Stay inside the time window



Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.








Important3. No leakage



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

Part 0: Setup

library(sf)

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""   # should print TRUE


[1] TRUE



The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}




The model log
Every time you fit a new model, add a row. By the end, this table is the story of your assignment.

  model   = character(),
  added   = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(),
  notes   = character()
)

  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",

    total_pop = "B01003_001",
    # your outcome's numerator and denominator (or median), e.g.:
    vehicle_hh = "B08201_001",
    no_vehicle = "B08201_002",
    # your baseline predictors, e.g.:
    median_income = "B19013_001",
    poverty_den = "B17001_001",
    poverty_num = "B17001_002",
    tenure_total = "B25003_001",
    renter = "B25003_003"

  year = 2023,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = TRUE,
  progress_bar = FALSE
) %>%
  st_transform(2272)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    # build your outcome, e.g. a percentage:
    y = no_vehicleE / vehicle_hhE * 100,
    
    # and its reliability. For a percentage, use tidycensus::moe_prop();
    # for a median or count, use the E and M columns directly.
    y_moe = tidycensus::moe_prop(
      num = no_vehicleE,
      denom = vehicle_hhE,
      moe_num = no_vehicleM,
      moe_denom = vehicle_hhM
    ) * 100,
    
    # coefficient of variation
    y_cv  = if_else(
      y > 0,
      (y_moe / 1.645) / y * 100,
      NA_real_
    ),
    
    # your predictors:
    poverty_pct = poverty_numE / poverty_denE *100,
    renter_pct = renterE / tenure_totalE * 100,
    
    reliability = case_when(
      is.na(y_cv) ~ "Missing",
      y_cv < 12 ~ "High",
      y_cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE ~ "Low"

section: Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary_2023)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.446  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)

5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.

Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer: The baseline model used median household income, poverty rate, and renter share to predict the percentage of households without a vehicle. Its cross-validated RMSE was approximately 11.94 percentage points. Among the spatial features, residential burglary density helped the most, reducing RMSE to approximately 11.22. I do not interpret burglary as causing households to live without vehicles. Instead, its density may capture urban intensity and neighborhood conditions not fully represented by the ACS predictors. The raw burglary count was the most disappointing feature, reducing RMSE only to approximately 11.73. Raw counts are affected by tract size, whereas density is more comparable across tracts. Combining the useful spatial features with a curved income relationship produced the best model, with an RMSE of approximately 10.74.
In the final model, the coefficient for renter share was approximately 0.294. The beta interpretation is that, holding poverty, income, burglary density, and distance to a SEPTA station constant, a one-percentage-point increase in renter share is associated with a 0.294-percentage-point increase in the predicted share of households without a vehicle. The y-hat interpretation is that two otherwise similar tracts differing by ten percentage points in renter share are predicted to differ by approximately 2.94 percentage points in their no-vehicle household shares.
The final residual map shows smaller errors in many areas, but a cluster of underprediction remains around central Philadelphia. A useful next feature would be transit service frequency and job accessibility. Distance to a station does not measure how often service arrives or which destinations can be reached. Historical 2023 SEPTA GTFS schedules could provide these measures.
Finally, the relationship between outcome CV and absolute final residual was nearly flat, with a correlation of approximately −0.05. This suggests that ACS sampling uncertainty explains little of the remaining error overall. Some residuals may contain statistical noise, but the remaining spatial pattern is more consistent with omitted transportation, land-use, and neighborhood characteristics.

[1] 153

  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

text:
The lab question: a housing agency wants an expected rent for every Philadelphia tract. This is a ŷ (y-hat) problem, not a β̂ (beta-hat) problem. ŷ = prediction: guess a number for each row. β̂ = inference: ask why / does X cause Y?
get_acs(… , geometry = TRUE) with more variables: med_rent = “B25064_001” # median gross rent (our Y) med_inc = “B19013_001” # median household income renter_occ, occ_units, education variables (ba, ma, prof, phd)

Count Indego stations within half a mile of each tract (Week 4 tools). In EPSG:2272, the units are US feet, so half a mile is 2,640 feet: st_is_within_distance(tracts, stations, dist = 2640) # returns a list, one element per tract lengths(…) # turns the list into a plain numeric vector: n_stations

Fit m2: lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations) Read one coefficient two ways:

β̂ reading: bike stations don’t “raise” rents; the coefficient soaks up neighborhood character (multicollinearity), so no causal claim.
ŷ reading: keep the variable if it helps guess rent on new tracts.

Check survey noise: plot abs(residual) vs rent_cv. Big miss + high CV = maybe survey noise, not model failure. Don’t trust those tracts.

Lower = better. # R² always rises when you add variables, so it can never tell you the new variables truly help.
Where is the model wrong? Residuals vs fitted + bptest(m2); map residuals with geom_sf(). Red = rent higher than predicted. Errors cluster (University City, Northeast): the model is missing something about those places.
Challenge: build the best rent prediction model. Lowest CV RMSE wins. Rule: no leakage — cannot use anything built from rent itself (med_rentM, rent_cv, rent burden…). title: Week 5: Intro into machine learning
text:
Key Concepts
This lab was an introduction to machine learning for prediction, using linear regression. The core distinction is prediction (ŷ) versus inference (β̂): prediction asks “what will Y be for a new row,” while inference asks “does X cause Y and by how much.” The same coefficient gets read two different ways depending on the task. For grading a prediction model we use out-of-sample error: split the data into train and test sets, or better, use k-fold cross-validation, and report RMSE — the typical miss in dollars on unseen data. In-sample R² always improves when variables are added, so it cannot judge whether new variables truly help; CV RMSE can get worse, which makes it the honest grade. I also learned that our Y itself is noisy: ACS rent estimates carry margins of error, and a large residual in a high-CV tract may be survey fog rather than signal. Finally, mapping residuals showed that errors are not random in space — they cluster — which means the model is missing real spatial structure.

title: Week 5: Intro into machine learning
text:
Reflection
This lab changed how I read regression output. Before, I thought a significant p-value meant a variable was “good.” Now I see the p-value answers the inference question, while prediction is graded by CV RMSE on data the model has never seen — and a variable can fail the first test but pass the second. Plotting the residuals on a map was the most surprising part: the red clusters made it obvious that the model doesn’t know something about University City and the Northeast, and no table of coefficients shows that as clearly. The hardest part is letting go of causal language: it feels natural to say “stations raise rents,” but for this task all that matters is whether the variable helps the guess.

title: Week 6: Regression Features for Prediction
text:
Set the chunk option progress = FALSE to hide the knitting progress bar.
Project City Hall into the planar CRS, so distances are calculated correctly at the urban scale:

city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(2272)  # from degrees to US feet

Deal with NA before fitting:

filter(!is.na(rent), !is.na(income), !is.na(bldg_age), !is.na(pct_renter))

The 10-fold cross-validated RMSE, our honest grade for every model in this lab:

cv_rmse <- function(f, data, log_outcome = FALSE) {
  preds <- numeric(nrow(data))
  for (k in 1:10) {
    m <- lm(f, data = data[folds != k, ])           # train on 9 folds
    p <- predict(m, newdata = data[folds == k, ])   # predict the held-out fold
    if (log_outcome) p <- exp(p)                    # back to dollars (more on this soon)
    preds[folds == k] <- p
  }
  sqrt(mean((data$rent - preds)^2))
}

cv_rmse(f0, tracts)  # the baseline model's honest grade




Why logs? Skew.
Log a predictor: Y = β·log(x) — a 1% increase in income goes with about β/100 dollars more rent, holding the other variables constant.

log1p(x)  # deal with x = 0

Log the outcome: log(y) = β·log(x) — a 1% increase in income goes with about β% change in rent (an elasticity).

cv_rmse(f_logy, tracts, log_outcome = TRUE)
# exp() the outcome so RMSE is compared in the same scale (dollars)




Add a squared term:

... + bldg_age + I(bldg_age^2)

If the turning point is outside your data, the curve is just bending, not turning.





Turn a continuous distance into an ordered factor:

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

Change the reference level:

tracts_r <- tracts %>%
  mutate(ring = relevel(ring, ref = "Outer"))
# often the largest group or a natural baseline




A plain categorical can only shift the line up or down (base). An interaction lets it tilt (delta).

# slope in Outer =
#     log(income)             # base
#   + log(income):ringOuter   # delta




Fixed effects allow each group, such as a planning district or neighborhood, to have its own intercept. In R, this is implemented by adding a factor to the model:

m_fe <- lm(rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter + district, data = tracts)

A factor with k groups becomes k − 1 dummy variables. Each coefficient compares one group with the reference group, holding the other predictors constant.
Fixed effects can improve prediction by capturing unmeasured group characteristics, but they do not explain which neighborhood feature matters. They can also overfit when groups contain very few rows.
Small groups should be combined before cross-validation. Otherwise, a test fold may contain a factor level that the training folds never saw, so the model cannot make a prediction for that level.
As with every other feature, keep fixed effects only when they improve cross-validated RMSE and still allow predictions for new observations.

Change the reference level:

tracts_r <- tracts %>%
  mutate(ring = relevel(ring, ref = "Outer"))
# often the largest group or a natural baseline




A plain categorical can only shift the line up or down (base). An interaction lets it tilt (delta).

# slope in Outer =
#     log(income)             # base
#   + log(income):ringOuter   # delta




Fixed effects allow each group, such as a planning district or neighborhood, to have its own intercept. In R, this is implemented by adding a factor to the model:

m_fe <- lm(rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter + district, data = tracts)

A factor with k groups becomes k − 1 dummy variables. Each coefficient compares one group with the reference group, holding the other predictors constant.
Fixed effects can improve prediction by capturing unmeasured group characteristics, but they do not explain which neighborhood feature matters. They can also overfit when groups contain very few rows.
Small groups should be combined before cross-validation. Otherwise, a test fold may contain a factor level that the training folds never saw, so the model cannot make a prediction for that level.
As with every other feature, keep fixed effects only when they improve cross-validated RMSE and still allow predictions for new observations.

title: Week 6: Regression Features for Prediction
text:
Key Concepts
This lab was about making the linear model more flexible, one feature at a time, and letting cross-validated RMSE judge each addition. Logs handle skew: logging a predictor means a 1% change in income goes with about β/100 dollars more rent, while logging the outcome too turns the coefficient into an elasticity (a β% change), and predictions must be exp()’d back to dollars before computing RMSE. Squared terms let the relationship bend, but the turning point has to sit inside the data range — otherwise the curve is just bending, not turning. Categorical predictors enter as dummies against a reference level, and relevel() lets me pick a more natural baseline such as the largest group. Interactions go further: a plain categorical only shifts the line (base), while an interaction lets it tilt (delta), so a group’s slope is the sum of two coefficients. The same cv_rmse() from Part 0 grades every version, with log_outcome = TRUE whenever the outcome was logged, and fixed effects extend this dummy-variable idea to many groups at once.

title: Week 6: Regression Features for Prediction
text:
Reflection
What stuck with me is how much the interpretation depends on where the log goes: β/100 dollars per 1% with only the predictor logged, an elasticity when both sides are logged, and dollars again only after exp() — the same model read three different ways. Reading an interaction as base + delta also made the coefficient table less intimidating, because the slope for the Outer ring is not one number but the sum of two. The turning-point check is a good guard against over-reading a squared term whose vertex sits far outside the sample. The hardest habit is restraint: a square, a factor, or an interaction each cost one line of code, but only CV RMSE decides whether they stay.

title: Week 6: Regression Features for Prediction
text:
Questions I Still Have
If relevel() only changes the reference group, the fitted values and CV RMSE should not move at all — how do I check that in practice? And for fixed effects: are they just dummy variables for many groups, and can they soak up so much variation that they hide the variables I actually care about?

title: Week 3: ggplot and More MOEs
text:
We got Census data in NY, calculated moe_pct and classified by confidence, plotted the data in different forms and decorated the plots.

Downloaded ACS county data, then calculated relative margin of error:


county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(
    moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
      moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
    )
  )


Used ggplot() to build charts. Variables placed inside aes() are mapped to the data. Fixed design choices, such as making every point blue, should normally go outside aes().


ggplot(county_data, aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")


Added error bars from estimate - moe to estimate + moe. We used arrange() and slice_head() to keep the 15 least reliable counties, reorder() to sort them, coord_flip() to make names readable, and str_remove() to shorten labels.


county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, " County, New York")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe),
    width = 0.3
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal()


Calculated uncertainty for derived values:

moe_sum() calculates the MOE for a combined total. We should not simply add the individual MOEs.
moe_prop() calculates the MOE for a proportion using uncertainty from both the numerator and denominator.

Compared ACS estimates over time. First convert each 90% MOE to a standard error with SE = MOE / 1.645. For two independent estimates:

\[
SE_{difference} = \sqrt{SE_1^2 + SE_2^2}
\]
Then calculate z = change / SE_difference. At the 90% confidence level, abs(z) > 1.645 indicates a statistically significant change.

Key Concepts


Original quick notes (kept)

point()
key functions: 
  ggplot(data): build a canvas, 
    aes(reorder()): sort
  aes(x, y): aesthetic mapping, no decorating, 
  slice_head(n): get the first 15,

Corrected function summary:

ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) creates the plot and maps variables to visual properties.
geom_point() draws points; geom_col() draws bars.
geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe)) shows uncertainty.
reorder(NAME, estimate) sorts categories by a numeric variable.
slice_head(n = 15) keeps the first 15 rows.
str_remove() removes unwanted text from labels.
labs() adds clear titles and axis labels.
coord_flip() swaps the axes.
theme_minimal() reduces unnecessary visual clutter.

Relative MOE and coefficient of variation are related but not identical:

moe_pct <- moe / estimate * 100
cv_pct  <- (moe / 1.645) / estimate * 100

Both help compare uncertainty across estimates of different sizes. Larger values mean lower reliability.

text:

Learned more about the meaning of moe_pct and how it reflects the information.
Using plot functions can make the plots more readable.

This practice also showed me that uncertainty must be carried through the analysis. When values are added, divided, or compared across time, their margins of error must be combined with the correct formula. A polished chart should show both the estimate and its uncertainty instead of hiding the MOE.

How to precisely define the confidence threshold
There is no single threshold that works for every project. The choice should depend on the policy question, geographic scale, sample size, and the cost of making a decision from an uncertain estimate. The threshold should be selected before looking for a preferred result and clearly reported.

title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text:
We predict single-family sale prices in Chicago from 2023 to 2025. Starting with a structure-only model, we add accessibility, neighborhood, property, and time features, then compare transformations using the same ten validation folds.
The selected model reduces mean ten-fold RMSE from $285,974 for the previous model to $250,171, a 12.5% improvement. The outcome remains the original sale price in dollars throughout. The comparison uses ordinary linear regression with the predictor logs, squared terms, categories, and interactions covered in class.

add('facility_interactions','Coordinate model + size by air-conditioning/single-story',paste(counts,curves,geo_terms,'building_000sf:central_air + building_000sf:one_story',sep=' + '))




2B: Try changes that have a reason
We first add the existing property, land, and sale-time attributes. We then compare raw versus logged predictors, squares of size and age, and grouped count variables. For location, we test linear coordinates, their squares, and their interaction; area-by-coordinate interactions allow an extra square foot to have different dollar value in different places. Centering longitude at −87.65 and latitude at 41.88 makes the coordinate terms easier to calculate and leaves their model information unchanged.
The alternative tract fixed-effect models use Census tracts as neighborhood categories. Within each training fold, tracts with fewer than 70 sales and unseen validation tracts are pooled into “Other,” following the lecture’s advice to merge sparse categories. No neighboring sale prices, residual lags, or other target-derived predictors are used.


Show code
prepare_fold<-function(tr,va) {
 vars<-c('lotsize_acre','num_half_baths','num_fireplaces','garage_size','warmairfurnace','full_basement')
 for(v in vars){med<-median(tr[[v]],na.rm=TRUE);tr[[v]][is.na(tr[[v]])]<-med;va[[v]][is.na(va[[v]])]<-med}
 # Keep sparse or unseen tract groups pooled; the group rule uses training X only.
 freq<-table(tr$GEOID);common<-names(freq)[freq>=70]
 tr$tract_group<-ifelse(!is.na(tr$GEOID)&tr$GEOID %in% common,tr$GEOID,'Other')
 va$tract_group<-ifelse(!is.na(va$GEOID)&va$GEOID %in% common,va$GEOID,'Other')
 add_variables <- function(x) {
  x$lon_c <- x$lon + 87.65
  x$lat_c <- x$lat - 41.88
  x$age_band <- cut(x$building_age,
    breaks = c(-Inf, 5, 20, 50, 80, 110, Inf), right = TRUE,
    labels = c('0-5', '6-20', '21-50', '51-80', '81-110', '111+'))
  x
 }
 tr <- add_variables(tr)
 va <- add_variables(va)
 list(tr=tr,va=va)
}
fit_predict<-function(cand,tr,va) {
 z<-prepare_fold(tr,va)
 f<-as.formula(paste('sale_price ~',cand$rhs))
 fit<-lm(f,data=z$tr)
 pred<-as.numeric(predict(fit,newdata=z$va))
 stopifnot(length(pred)==nrow(va),all(is.finite(pred)))
 list(pred=pred,fit=fit)
}
score<-function(cand,folds,seed=5080) {
 pred<-rep(NA_real_,nrow(d));fr<-numeric(length(folds))
 for(k in seq_along(folds)) {
  ti<-folds[[k]];vi<-setdiff(seq_len(nrow(d)),ti)
  pred[vi]<-fit_predict(cand,d[ti,],d[vi,])$pred
  fr[k]<-sqrt(mean((d$sale_price[vi]-pred[vi])^2))
 }
 e<-d$sale_price-pred
 metrics<-data.frame(model=cand$id,description=cand$description,seed=seed,
  cv_rmse=mean(fr),pooled_rmse=sqrt(mean(e^2)),mae=mean(abs(e)),median_ae=median(abs(e)),
  oof_r2=1-sum(e^2)/sum((d$sale_price-mean(d$sale_price))^2),
  moran_i=as.numeric(moran(e,w,n=length(e),S0=Szero(w))$I),negative_oof=sum(pred<0))
 list(metrics=metrics,pred=pred)
}

text:
Part 6: Reflection


Show code
air_beta <- unname(coef(final_fit$fit)["central_air"])


The central-air coefficient is $9,555. Holding the other modeled features fixed, houses with central air are associated with a sale price that is $9,555 higher. For prediction, otherwise identical input records differing only in central air receive predictions that differ by this same dollar amount. This association does not establish the causal effect of installing air conditioning.
The useful changes: logs compress a predictor’s long tail, squares allow a curved relationship, factors allow category differences, and interactions let a relationship vary by place. We keep the outcome in dollars so the model coefficients, predictions, and RMSE remain in dollar units. Better-looking predictor distributions alone are not enough; each choice is assessed using the same validation procedure.
We would not yet deploy the model for assessments. Expensive or unusual transactions still have large errors, residuals remain spatially clustered, and some forecasts are negative. Validation uses random folds rather than future-year or geographic holdouts, and unsold properties may differ from the observed sales. These limitations should accompany the lower CV RMSE.

Question 2.1: Why a grid instead of Chicago’s 77 community areas? Give two reasons.
Your answer: A regular grid provides a finer spatial resolution than Chicago’s 77 community areas, allowing us to identify local patterns within neighborhoods. It also uses cells of a consistent size and shape, making spatial comparisons more consistent.
Question 2.2: Why did you pick that cell size? Name one thing that would change if you doubled it.
Your answer: I chose 500 feet to match the scale used in the Philadelphia example and capture local variation. Doubling the cell size to 1,000 feet would quadruple each full cell’s area, generally increasing counts per cell and smoothing local patterns.

Question 3.1: What share of cells have zero burglaries? Give two reasons, from the slides, that OLS will struggle here.
Your answer: 77.8 % of cells have zero burglaries. OLS can produce negative predictions for nonnegative counts, and its constant-variance assumption is poorly suited to sparse counts whose variance changes with their expected level.
Question 3.2: Compare the mean and the variance. What does a Poisson model assume about them, and does Chicago meet that assumption?
Your answer: The mean is 0.36, and the variance is 0.88. A Poisson model assumes that the conditional variance equals the conditional mean. Part 4: Features from 2024
Build one of each feature type. These are the same four types as in A4.

centroids <- st_centroid(fishnet)

knn_dist <- function(from, to, k) {
  nn <- get.knnx(st_coordinates(to), st_coordinates(from), k = k)
  rowMeans(nn$nn.dist)
}

# The Loop: State & Madison
loop <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-87.6278, 41.8820)), crs = 4326) %>% st_transform(crs_chi)

fishnet <- fishnet %>%
  mutate(
    cars_cnt     = lengths(st_intersects(., abandoned_cars)),          # count in cell
    light_nn1    = knn_dist(centroids, light_outages, k = 1),       # nearest distance
    graffiti_nn3 = knn_dist(centroids, graffiti, k = 3),       # kNN distance
    loop_mi      = as.numeric(st_distance(centroids, loop)) / 5280,
    log_light_nn1    = log(light_nn1),
    log_graffiti_nn3 = log(graffiti_nn3)
  )

Question 4.1: Why do we log the distances but not cars_cnt?
Your answer: Logging distances reduces the influence of very large values and allows the effect of an additional foot to diminish with distance. We keep cars_cnt in its original scale to model changes per additional complaint and retain zero counts, since log(0) is undefined.

title: Lab 9: Predicting Burglary in Chicago
section: Part 7B: Does it beat last year’s map?
text:
Part 7B: Does it beat last year’s map?
Before any model, departments smoothed last year’s burglaries into a heat map and patrolled the hot parts. Your model has to beat that.

library(spatstat.geom)
library(spatstat.explore)

bb  <- st_bbox(fishnet)   # use the fishnet's extent, so every cell centroid falls inside the window
win <- owin(xrange = c(bb["xmin"], bb["xmax"]), yrange = c(bb["ymin"], bb["ymax"]))

xy_2024  <- st_coordinates(st_filter(burg_2024, chicago))   # which year? drop points outside the city
kde_2024 <- density(ppp(xy_2024[, 1], xy_2024[, 2], window = win), sigma = 1000)  # 1000 ft

xy_cent <- st_coordinates(centroids)
fishnet$kde_2024 <- safelookup(kde_2024, ppp(xy_cent[, 1], xy_cent[, 2], window = win))

You’ll probably see a warning about duplicated points. That’s expected: Chicago geocodes crimes to the block, not the address, so many incidents share coordinates.
Now take the top 10% of cells by each method and count how many of 2025’s burglaries fall inside:

fishnet %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(model_top = pred_pois >= quantile(pred_pois, 0.9),
         kde_top   = kde_2024  >= quantile(kde_2024, 0.9)) %>%
  summarize(model = sum(burglaries[model_top]) / sum(burglaries),
            kde   = sum(burglaries[kde_top])   / sum(burglaries))

      model       kde
1 0.2668667 0.3046358


Question 7B.1: Which method captured more of 2025’s burglaries in its top 10% of cells? By how much?
Your answer: The KDE captured more of 2025’s burglaries in its top 10% of cells: 30.5 % compared with 26.7 %, a difference of 3.8 percentage points.
Question 7B.2: This comparison is rigged in the model’s favor. Explain why. (Hint: which of the two has already seen the 2025 data?)
Your answer: The comparison favors the Poisson model because it was trained and evaluated on the same 2025 burglary counts, while the KDE used only 2024 data. Despite this in-sample advantage, the model still captured fewer burglaries than the KDE.
Question 7B.3: If the model only beats last year’s map by a little, what are you getting in exchange for its extra complexity and its extra sources of bias?
Your answer: In my results, the model actually performed worse than the KDE, so its extra complexity did not improve this measure of performance. It also requires additional data and introduces potential bias from differences in 311 reporting behavior. These results favor the simpler KDE for this task, although both methods should be evaluated on unseen future data.
